name: Nunggubuyu
confidence_why: Hore 1981, Heath 1984, Baker et al. 2019 and Nyhuis 2023 all place main stress on the penult of words with short vowels, but Hore 1981, Heath 1984 and Nyhuis 2023 also have a long vowel attract it (a long final syllable is stressed), so the strict penultimate coding is a simplification and the placement is only firm for short-vowel words.
catalog_quote: Stress is usually penultimate. Secondary stress occurs on the initial syllable and every other syllable thereafter. There are exceptions in which long vowels seem to attract stress.Phonetic cues for stress are intensity, pitch and duration. (Hore 1981)
sweep_summary: Wubuy/Nunggubuyu (nung1290): both works with stress in the title are the same work, Hore 1981 (Glottolog 129129 and a year-less duplicate 316019 with a wrong '1-102' page range; the paper is pp. 1-62). It was already held by the project (AuSIL open PDF, scanned; link re-verified live 2026-09-17) and was read first-hand this search of works with stress in the title. Hore p. 13 states the pattern the catalog paraphrases (penult primary, alternating secondary from syllable 1) but p. 14 makes long syllables rule-governed heavy units that take stress (ma\"gaa final, \"daabulu initial), and rule 17 (p. 36) puts primary stress on the last stress of the STEM, so suffixed words are stem-penult ('warru.\"burruyung). Hence the catalog's 'fixed-strict' coding is contradicted; the right coding is weight-sensitive (long vowel = heavy), penult default, stem-bounded. Also read: Heath 1984 §2.11 (hedged, intonation-first; long vowels attract stress, penult otherwise), Baker et al. 2019 ICPhS (instrumental; penult fits trisyllabic all-short roots better than closed-syllable weight, long vowels excluded, 'quantity-sensitive stress remain[s] elusive'), Nyhuis 2023 PhD ch. 6 (AM corpus study: right-edge accent on the syllable containing the penultimate mora, final if long else penult; treats prominence as post-lexical), and newly downloaded Ryan & Heath 2022 AMP (reduplication; silent on stress placement). Not obtained: Jepson & Ennever 2023 OUP survey chapter (paywalled DOI, medium priority) and Baker et al. 2020 LabPhon17 talk (no copy found, low). Crossref title search and direct download were used instead. New file and line

new_statements.quote: p. 13: 'for words with short syllables only, the normal situation is that the first and penultimate syllables are stressed as well as the third, fifth etc. syllables, depending on the length of the word. ... The penultimate syllable receives the primary stress.' p. 14: 'Long syllables can be accounted for quite easily. Basically, each S: forms a stress group of its own; where, however, the S: is preceded or followed by a single S, the S can be included in the same stress group as the S:. The S: usually retains the stress when this occurs.'
new_statements.citation: Hore, Michael. 1981. Syllable length and stress in Nunggubuyu. In Bruce Waters (ed.), Australian phonologies: collected papers (Work Papers of SIL-AAB, Series A, Vol. 5), 1-62. Darwin: SIL-AAB.
new_statements.locator: pp. 13-14 (PDF pp. 27-28), section 2.2 'Stress groups'; supporting: p. 15-16 word lists (ma"gaa, "daabulu), p. 29 exx. 20-22, p. 36 rule 17
new_statements.reading: Primary stress on the penult of all-short words with secondary stress on syllables 1, 3, 5 (left-to-right alternation); long-vowel syllables are heavy, form their own stress group and take stress, so CVCVV words are final-stressed (ma"gaa) and S:SS words initial-stressed ("daabulu); primary stress is the last stress of the stem (rule 17), so suffixes leave it in place ('warru."burruyung). Coding: weight-sensitive (long vowel = heavy), right-edge/penult default, stem-bounded; NOT fixed-strict. Nyhuis 2023 (corpus AM study) corroborates the right-edge weight rule in modern terms: accent on the syllable containing the penultimate mora, i.e. final if long, else penult.

audit.recode_to: weight-hedged (right edge; heavy = long vowel): primary stress on the penult by default, but a long-vowel syllable attracts stress — word-final long vowel takes primary (Hore ma"gaa, 'mundu."gaa; Heath /nga=ngu-yí:/; Nyhuis 2023: right-edge accent on the syllable containing the penultimate MORA, i.e. final if long, penult otherwise), initial long vowel in S:SS words takes primary ("daabulu, "maalamburrg); secondary on the initial syllable and alternately thereafter in all-short words (Hore p. 13), with word-initial SSS sometimes initial-stressed ("wurrugu, "marriya). not in the strict set. Add caution: Heath 1984 and Nyhuis 2023 regard word-level prominence as largely intonational/edge-marking (left edges of morphological constituents + AP-final accent) and doubt a separate lexical stress system; Baker et al. 2019 instrumental test of penult-vs-weight was inconclusive. 'weight' (unhedged) is defensible on Hore 1981 alone; 'fixed-strict' is not supported by any first-hand source.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. i: 'I also find evidence of a pitch accent that aligns to the right edge of the verb, and does so in a way indicative of quantity-sensitivity: it anchors to the final syllable of the word if it is heavy, and to the penultimate otherwise.' p. 389: 'this Accentual Phrase is tonally marked at its right edge by means of a pitch accent anchored to its penultimate mora, which is to be found in the final syllable when it is long, and the penultimate otherwise.'
sources.locator: Abstract p. i; ch. 6 §6.2 pp. 341-342 (review of Heath 1984 and Hore 1981); §6.6 conclusion (the text layer); ch. 7 p. 389
sources.note: Most recent first-hand study: AM analysis of an unscripted narrative corpus. Pitch accents optional, aligned to left edges of morphological constituents (root, reduplication base, stem, word) plus an AP-final accent on the syllable containing the penultimate mora (final if long, else penult). Nyhuis treats prominence as post-lexical/intonational and doubts a separate lexical stress system (calls Hore's 'stress group' 'a fairly nebulous theoretical construct', p. 342). For the catalog: right-edge, penult by default, long-vowel weight-sensitive; not 'strict'.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 2730: 'The other hypothesis is that stress is simply associated with penultimate position, as in [9].' ... 'We excluded long vowels from the analysis because there were insufficient numbers to validly test the effect of long vowels on acoustic correlates.' p. 2732: 'The second, following [9], predicts consistent penultimate stress in trisyllabic roots. On balance, the second hypothesis receives more support from the acoustic measures tested with this dataset, although the picture is not fully consistent.' ... 'the existence and correlates of quantity-sensitive stress remain elusive.'
sources.note: Instrumental test on trisyllabic noun roots (3 speakers, frame-final): penultimate-position hypothesis (attributed to Hore [9]) fits the acoustics somewhat better than a closed-syllable-weight metrical hypothesis, but long-vowel tokens were excluded, F0 looks like a phrasal boundary tone (HL%/HH%) rather than lexical accent, and the authors call quantity-sensitive stress 'elusive'. Supports penult default in all-short trisyllables; silent on long-vowel weight; does not license 'strict'.
